sentences.text: Ikanogavialis possessed an extremely elongated snout that comprised more than 80% of its total skull length.
Its mouth featured very numerous teeth oriented horizontally, resembling a sawfish, with 30 on each maxilla and 31 on each dentary.
The type species I. gameroi was named in 1970 based on fossils found in the Urumaco Formation of Venezuela.
Ikanogavialis is classified within the subfamily Gryposuchinae.
A 2007 phylogenetic analysis placed Ikanogavialis within the subfamily Gryposuchinae alongside genera such as Aktiogavialis, Gryposuchus, Piscogavialis, and Siquisiquesuchus.
Ikanogavialis lived from the Langhian to the Messinian stages, approximately 15.98 to 5.333 million years ago.
The strata containing Ikanogavialis remains are late Miocene in age, correcting earlier beliefs that they were Pliocene.
Ikanogavialis likely lived in a coastal paleoenvironment alongside other gavialids like Gryposuchus.

It is debated whether the Pleistocene gavialoid from Woodlark Island, Papua New Guinea, belongs to Ikanogavialis, as it was originally named Gavialis papuensis in 1905 but the poor fossil quality makes determination difficult.
The proposal to refer the Pleistocene form Gavialis papuensis to Ikanogavialis is not widely accepted.
A 2018 study suggests that Gryposuchinae, including Ikanogavialis, may be paraphyletic and represent an evolutionary grade leading to Gavialis and the gharial.
